header.tag_why: The trigger was a broken buy-online-return-in-store flow and split customer records, and the store side chose the vendor that pitched one platform for the tills and the website. On a live return at the till, a rollout plan and who does the installs, we offered descriptions and a partner instead of proof and people.

messaging_changes.current_line: Online and in-store on one platform; the line between them has pretty much disappeared.
messaging_changes.change: For retail buyers with stores, say: One system for your tills and your website: one customer, one basket. Back it with a live, step-by-step demo of an online order being returned at a store till, with the same customer record carrying through to loyalty. If we can't show the till return, don't lead with this line. Say "the tills", not "in-person payments" or "point of sale".
messaging_changes.why: Store ops dismissed our M3 line as "that's a diagram" and asked to watch a return at the till, which we only described, while the customer framed the problem in their own words ("One system for the tills and the website.", "one customer, one basket.") around the returns and split-record failure that started the deal.

messaging_changes.change: For COO and store-operations buyers, add a rollout and accountability proof point: One team accountable for your stores, end to end: a rollout plan with dates, who installs, what happens to the old tills, and who shows up when a till goes down. If a partner does the installs, name the single point of contact and state that we stay accountable, so the buyer is never left with "two vendors pointing at each other".
messaging_changes.why: The decider said "I don't want two vendors pointing at each other.", and our answer to who does the installs was a partner; we also never produced the rollout plan they asked for, while Adyen brought people who had done store rollouts and most of the customer's questions were about stores.

messaging_changes.current_line: Trusted by leading businesses; see our customer stories.
messaging_changes.change: For retail buyers, replace the case-study link with an offer to talk to a peer: Talk to a retailer running their tills and website with us. Use this only when a reference retailer is confirmed and available to take the call quickly, so we can set it up when asked.
messaging_changes.why: The decider asked "can I talk to them?" and we couldn't set up a call in time, while Adyen named retailers she knew, so pointing to customer stories was not the proof she wanted.

evidence.excerpt: Returns. Last holiday season. Buy online, return in store. The store couldn't see the online order
evidence.label: fact
evidence.speaker: rep

evidence.excerpt: they'd just launched a loyalty program that was supposed to work everywhere and didn't, because store and web were two different customer records
evidence.label: fact
evidence.speaker: rep

evidence.excerpt: Their COO, Angela, apparently stood in a store on December 27th watching the returns queue. That's the story everybody there tells.
evidence.label: opinion
evidence.speaker: rep

trigger.insight: The pain started in the stores: returns at the till and a loyalty program broken by split customer records. It was not a checkout or conversion problem. Even so, by the rep's account the customer's questions were all web until they met Adyen, and our strongest moment was the online checkout demo. We sold to the evaluation's early framing, not to the problem that started it. The origin story the company tells puts the COO in a store returns queue, which pointed to the eventual signer from day one.
trigger.messaging: For retail deals, open with the trigger scenario itself (an online order returned at a store till, with one customer record for loyalty), not with M1's global, every-currency positioning.

decider.insight: The rep named Raj because he ran the RFP and was the rep's contact. When pressed, the rep conceded that Angela signed with Adyen and that her stores team asked for the workshop that sank us. We met the signer once, at kickoff. Our read that we were ahead rested entirely on a contact who did not sign, and even Raj's support is hedged.
decider.messaging: Retail messaging needs a COO and store-operations track built on operational risk, returns and rollout accountability, alongside the CTO-oriented developer and checkout story (M2).

competitor.insight: Everything we know about Adyen came from Raj after the deal, and none of it concerns product capability. It concerns people who had done store rollouts, the customer's own words ('the tills and the website'), 'one contract', and peers the decider knew. After they met Adyen, 11 of 14 questions were about stores: wifi drops, a 120-store rollout, who shows up on a Saturday. Adyen moved the evaluation onto the ground where the trigger lived. Whether Adyen actually demonstrated a till return is unknown.
competitor.messaging: Answer the store-operations questions in the pitch itself: who rolls out, who shows up when a till goes down, and what sits on one contract. Lead with retail peers the buyer can call, rather than a platform claim.

message.insight: Our web demo landed with the ecommerce lead, who did not decide the deal. M3, the message aimed squarely at this customer's pain, met silence and was dismissed by store ops as 'that's a diagram'. The hedge 'pretty much disappeared' is an abstraction to someone who watched returns fail at the till. Bev's follow-up was a request to see a return 'Step by step. At the till.', and the rep answered with a description. That pattern repeats throughout the deal.
message.messaging: Replace M3's claim slide with a step-by-step, demonstrable walkthrough of an online order returned at a store till. If we can't show it, don't lead with it.

decided.insight: The store ops workshop, requested by Angela's team, was the real evaluation. We brought two people with no store rollout experience to face six store-operations staff. 'we'd bring in a partner' is exactly the two-vendor setup Angela said she didn't want ('two vendors pointing at each other'), so the answer to who does the installs likely disqualified us on the spot. The 'we were ahead' read came from Raj and from the web side, after the questions had already shifted to stores.
decided.messaging: When we name a partner for installs or rollout, the messaging must state who is accountable end to end and who the single point of contact is. Without that, we are pitching the two-vendor problem the buyer is trying to escape.

gaps.insight: All three asks were proof requests from the store side: a retailer to call, a rollout plan, and a live till return. Each got a document, nothing, or a description. M8's case-study approach failed against a decider who wanted a conversation, while Adyen named retailers she already knew. The live return was the trigger scenario itself, and we never showed it. Why the reference call couldn't happen in time is not established.
gaps.messaging: Change M8 from 'see our customer stories' to an offer of a call with a retailer running stores and online on us. Have a till-return demo and a rollout plan template ready before any store workshop.

evidence.excerpt: They never said "unified commerce." We kept saying "in-person payments" and "point of sale." They said "the tills."
evidence.label: fact
evidence.speaker: rep

language.insight: The customer described their problem in concrete, physical terms: 'the tills', 'one customer, one basket', and accountability ('two vendors pointing at each other'). We kept saying 'unified commerce', 'in-person payments' and 'point of sale'. By Raj's account, Adyen spoke the customer's language back ('one platform for the tills and the website, on one contract'). Angela's line is about who is accountable, not about features.
language.messaging: Rewrite M3 for retail in the buyer's words, for example one system for your tills and your website, one customer, one basket, and state plainly who is accountable when something breaks.

gaps.question: Who made the final call, and how do you know?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Tom: did Raj ever say who held signing authority, and what did Angela weigh in the final decision? If possible, run a win-loss call with Raj or Angela.

gaps.question: What did you say when Bev asked how a return works at the till?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Tom and the solutions engineer: what exactly did you describe, and could we have demonstrated a till return live if given time?

gaps.question: Did Raj genuinely back us, and on what basis?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Tom what Raj said and when. If Raj is open to it, ask him directly what the web team's view was in the final decision.

gaps.question: Did Adyen demonstrate a live return at a till or show a rollout plan?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Raj (via Tom) what Adyen actually showed in their store sessions, as opposed to what they claimed.

gaps.question: Why couldn't we set up the reference call in time, and how much time did we have?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Tom and customer marketing: when did Angela ask, which retailer did we approach, and what blocked the call?

gaps.question: What did the customer use before (store and web providers)?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Tom which systems ran the tills and the website before, and whether contract timing with them played a role.

gaps.question: Did Adyen win both web and stores, or is any part of the business still open?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Tom whether the Adyen contract covers web as well as stores, and whether any part of the business is still open to us.

close.rep_takeaway: When a buyer asks to see something, describing it counts as a no. Bev asked to watch a return at the till and Angela asked to talk to a retailer, and both got words. Also follow the trigger to its owner: the problem began in Angela's stores, so she was the person to sell to, not only the CTO who ran the RFP. One meeting with the signer is a red flag to raise early, not discover afterwards.
